title: Two ways to land a track
summary: Trunk-based keeps history linear by rebasing a short-lived branch; feature-branch keeps every pushed commit and merges. Press Tour, or flip the setting in Workflow settings.

nodes.label: Branch from origin/main
nodes.detail:
```
git fetch origin
git switch -c <track_id> origin/main
```
Short-lived: hours to a few days.

nodes.label: Commit per setting
nodes.detail: Per task, phase or track (`git.commit`). Commits are local until the push rule says otherwise.

nodes.label: Fetch + rebase
nodes.detail:
```
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
```
Replays your commits on top of the latest main. Conflicts are resolved commit by commit, and history stays a straight line.

nodes.label: Push with lease
nodes.detail:
```
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes origin <track_id>
```
Rebasing rewrote the branch, so it needs a force push. **With lease**: refuses if someone else pushed to it since you fetched. **If-includes**: also refuses if you never integrated their work. **Only ever on your own track branch.**

nodes.label: Fast-forward main
nodes.detail: Rebase-merge or fast-forward into `main`, then delete the branch. `main` is never force-pushed.

nodes.label: Branch from main
nodes.detail:
```
git switch -c <track_id> main
```
Can live longer; nothing gets rewritten.

nodes.label: Push normally
nodes.detail:
```
git push -u origin <track_id>
```
No force, ever. Pushed history is permanent.

nodes.label: Merge commit
nodes.detail:
```
git switch main && git pull
git merge --no-ff <track_id>
```
Or through a pull request. The merge commit records when the track landed.

nodes.label: main (with merges)
nodes.detail: History shows the branch shape. Easier to see what landed together; noisier to read.
